plain_english: My first book, Novatus, had an easier topic to work with. It's like rolling a cart downhill — much simpler. Now we have to tackle drier, harder material. The question before us is this: does anger come from deliberate choice, or from impulse? In other words, does it act on its own, or is it like most other emotions that spring up inside us without our knowledge? We need to work through these basic matters first, so we can rise to higher themes later. Think of it like building a body. First you set the bones, tendons, and joints in place. They're not pretty to look at, but they're the foundation that keeps everything alive. Next come the parts that create all the beauty of face and appearance. Finally, you add color — the thing that charms the eye most of all — but only after the rest of the body is complete.
original_excerpt: My first book, Novatus, had a more abundant subject: for carriages roll easily down hill:[1] now we must proceed to drier matters. The question before us is whether anger arises from deliberate choice or from impulse, that is, whether it acts of its own accord or like the greater part of those passions which spring up within us without our knowledge. It is necessary for our debate to stoop to the consideration of these matters, in order that it may afterwards be able to rise to loftier themes; for likewise in our bodies the parts which are first set in order are the bones, sinews, and joints, which are by no means fair to see, albeit they are the foundation of our frame and essential to its life: next to them come the parts of which all beauty of face and appearance consists; and after these, colour, which above all else charms the eye, is applied last of all, when the rest of the body is complete.

plain_english:
There's no doubt that anger is triggered when we think someone has wronged us. But here's the question: Does anger follow immediately from that impression, springing up without any help from our thinking mind? Or does anger need our mind's agreement to get started?

We Stoics believe that anger can't do anything by itself without the mind's approval. Think about it: recognizing that a wrong has been done, wanting revenge, and connecting these two ideas — 'I shouldn't have been hurt' and 'I must get payback' — these can't come from a simple impulse that happens without our consent. A basic impulse is simple. But this anger process is complex, made up of several parts.

Here's what happens: A person notices something has occurred. He gets indignant about it. He judges the action as wrong. Then he seeks revenge. All of these steps can't happen without his mind agreeing to the thoughts that affected him.
original_excerpt: There is no doubt that anger is roused by the appearance of an injury being done: but the question before us is, whether anger straightway follows the appearance, and springs up without assistance from the mind, or whether it is roused with the sympathy of the mind. Our (the Stoics') opinion is, that anger can venture upon nothing by itself, without the approval of mind: for to conceive the idea of a wrong having been done, to long to avenge it, and to join the two propositions, that we ought not to have been injured and that it is our duty to avenge our injuries, cannot belong to a mere impulse which is excited without our consent. That impulse is a simple act; this is a complex one, and composed of several parts. The man understands something to have happened: he becomes indignant thereat: he condemns the deed; and he avenges it. All these things cannot be done without his mind agreeing to those matters which touched him.

plain_english: Where is this going, you ask? We need to understand what anger really is. If anger happens against our will, then reason will never defeat it. All movements that happen without our choice are beyond our control and unavoidable. We shiver when cold water hits us. We flinch when touched in sensitive spots. Our hair stands up at bad news. Our faces turn red at crude words. We get dizzy looking down a cliff. Since we can't prevent any of these things, no amount of reasoning will stop them. But anger can be driven away by wisdom. It's a voluntary flaw of the mind — not one of those things that just comes with being human and can happen even to the wisest people.
original_excerpt: Whither, say you, does this inquiry tend? That we may know what anger is: for if it springs up against our will, it never will yield to reason: because all the motions which take place without our volition are beyond our control and unavoidable, such as shivering when cold water is poured over us, or shrinking when we are touched in certain places. Men's hair rises up at bad news, their faces blush at indecent words, and they are seized with dizziness when looking down a precipice; and as it is not in our power to prevent any of these things, no reasoning can prevent their taking place. But anger can be put to flight by wise maxims; for it is a voluntary defect of the mind, and not one of those things which are evolved by the conditions of human life, and which, therefore, may happen even to the wisest of us.

plain_english: First on our list is that mental thrill we get when we think about wrongdoing. We feel this even when watching plays or reading about ancient history. We often get angry at Clodius for exiling Cicero, and at Antonius for killing him. Who isn't outraged by Marius's wars or Sulla's death lists? Who doesn't rage against Theodotus and Achillas and that boy king who committed such an adult crime? Sometimes songs stir us up, along with fast rhythms and the martial sound of trumpets. Disturbing pictures and terrible scenes of torture affect our minds too, even when the punishment is deserved. This is why we smile when others smile, why a crowd of mourners makes us sad, and why we get fired up about someone else's battles. None of these feelings are actually anger — any more than the frown we get watching a stage shipwreck is real sadness, or what we feel reading about Hannibal threatening Rome after Cannae is real fear. These are just stirrings in minds that don't want to be moved. They're not full passions, but seeds that could grow into passions. A soldier jumps at a trumpet's sound even when he's in civilian clothes during peacetime. War horses perk up their ears at the clash of weapons. They say Alexander reached for his sword when Xenophantus was singing.
original_excerpt: Among these and in the first place must be ranked that thrill of the mind which seizes us at the thought of wrongdoing. We feel this even when witnessing the mimic scenes of the stage, or when reading about things that happened long ago. We often feel angry with Clodius for banishing Cicero, and with Antonius for murdering him. Who is not indignant with the wars of Marius, the proscriptions of Sulla? who is not enraged against Theodotus and Achillas and the boy king who dared to commit a more than boyish crime?[2] Sometimes songs excite us, and quickened rhythm and the martial noise of trumpets; so, too, shocking pictures and the dreadful sight of tortures, however well deserved, affect our minds. Hence it is that we smile when others are smiling, that a crowd of mourners makes us sad, and that we take a glowing interest in another's battles; all of which feelings are not anger, any more than that which clouds our brow at the sight of a stage shipwreck is sadness, or what we feel, when we read how Hannibal after Cannae beset the walls of Rome, can be called fear. All these are emotions of minds which are loth to be moved, and are not passions, but rudiments which may grow into passions. So, too, a soldier starts at the sound of a trumpet, although he may be dressed as a civilian and in the midst of a profound peace, and camp horses prick up their ears at the clash of arms. It is said that Alexander, when Xenophantus was singing, laid his hand upon his weapons.

plain_english: None of these things that randomly affect our minds should be called true emotions. The mind doesn't create these feelings — it just lets them happen to it. Real passion isn't about being affected by what we see around us. It's about giving in to those feelings and chasing after these random impulses. If you think that turning pale, bursting into tears, feeling lust, sighing deeply, or having your eyes flash with anger are signs of real passion that show what's in your mind, you're wrong. You don't understand that these are just bodily reactions. That's why the bravest man often turns pale while putting on his armor. When the battle signal sounds, even the boldest soldier's knees shake for a moment. Even a great general's heart jumps into his throat just before the armies clash. Even the most eloquent speaker's hands and feet go stiff and cold while preparing to give a speech.
original_excerpt: None of these things which casually influence the mind deserve to be called passions: the mind, if I may so express it, rather suffers passions to act upon itself than forms them. A passion, therefore, consists not in being affected by the sights which are presented to us, but in giving way to our feelings and following up these chance promptings: for whoever imagines that paleness, bursting into tears, lustful feelings, deep sighs, sudden flashes of the eyes, and so forth, are signs of passion and betray the state of the mind, is mistaken, and does not understand that these are merely impulses of the body. Consequently, the bravest of men often turns pale while he is putting on his armour; when the signal for battle is given, the knees of the boldest soldier shake for a moment; the heart even of a great general leaps into his mouth just before the lines clash together, and the hands and feet even of the most eloquent orator grow stiff and cold while he is preparing to begin his speech.

plain_english: Anger doesn't just move you — it breaks all boundaries. It's an impulse. And no impulse can happen without your mind's consent. You can't deal with revenge and punishment without your mind knowing about it. A man might think someone has wronged him. He might want revenge. Then some reason convinces him to give up the idea and calm down. I don't call that anger. That's just an emotion controlled by reason. Anger is what goes beyond reason and drags reason along with it. So when your mind first gets confused after what seems like an injury — that's not anger any more than the apparent injury itself is. It's the crazy rush that comes next that is anger. This rush not only receives the impression of the apparent injury, but treats it as real and acts on it. Anger is the mind getting excited about revenge through choice and deliberate decision. No one has ever doubted that fear makes us run away, and anger makes us rush forward. So think about this: do you believe anything can be either pursued or avoided without your mind taking part?
original_excerpt: Anger must not merely move, but break out of bounds, being an impulse: now, no impulse can take place without the consent of the mind: for it cannot be that we should deal with revenge and punishment without the mind being cognisant of them. A man may think himself injured, may wish to avenge his wrongs, and then may be persuaded by some reason or other to give up his intention and calm down: I do not call that anger, it is an emotion of the mind which is under the control of reason. Anger is that which goes beyond reason and carries her away with it: wherefore the first confusion of a man’s mind when struck by what seems an injury is no more anger than the apparent injury itself: it is the subsequent mad rush, which not only receives the impression of the apparent injury, but acts upon it as true, that is anger, being an exciting of the mind to revenge, which proceeds from choice and deliberate resolve. There never has been any doubt that fear produces flight, and anger a rush forward; consider, therefore, whether you suppose that anything can be either sought or avoided without the participation of the mind.

plain_english: So you can understand how emotions start and build up and take over, let me explain how it works. The first stage is involuntary — it's like your mind getting ready for an emotion, or being threatened by one. The second stage includes wanting something, though not stubbornly yet. For example: "I should get revenge because someone hurt me," or "This person deserves punishment because they committed a crime." The third stage is already out of our control. It overpowers reason and wants revenge no matter what — not because it's right, but just because. We can't use reason to escape that first mental reaction, any more than we can escape certain physical reactions. We can't stop ourselves from yawning when others yawn. We can't help blinking when fingers suddenly dart toward our eyes. Reason can't overcome these habits. Maybe practice and constant attention could weaken them. But they're different from emotions, which we create and end through deliberate mental choices.
original_excerpt: Furthermore, that you may know in what manner passions begin and swell and gain spirit, learn that the first emotion is involuntary, and is, as it were, a preparation for a passion, and a threatening of one. The next is combined with a wish, though not an obstinate one, as, for example, “It is my duty to avenge myself, because I have been injured,” or “It is right that this man should be punished, because he has committed a crime.” The third emotion is already beyond our control, because it overrides reason, and wishes to avenge itself, not if it be its duty, but whether or no. We are not able by means of reason to escape from that first impression on the mind, any more than we can escape from those things which we have mentioned as occurring to the body: we cannot prevent other people’s yawns temping us to yawn:[3] we cannot help winking when fingers are suddenly darted at our eyes. Reason is unable to overcome these habits, which perhaps might be weakened by practice and constant watchfulness: they differ from an emotion which is brought into existence and brought to an end by a deliberate mental act.

plain_english: We should also ask about people whose cruelty has no limits. They love spilling human blood. Are they angry when they kill people who never hurt them — people they don't even think wronged them? Take men like Apollodorus or Phalaris. This isn't anger anymore. It's savagery. They don't hurt people because they were hurt first. They're willing to be hurt themselves if it means they get to hurt others. They don't want to beat and torture bodies for revenge. They do it for fun. So what's happening here? This evil grows out of anger. When anger gets fed and pampered for a long time, it makes a person forget mercy. It drives out all sense of human connection. Finally, it becomes cruelty. These men laugh and have a good time. They enjoy themselves immensely. They look nothing like angry people — because cruelty has become their entertainment.
original_excerpt: We must also enquire whether those whose cruelty knows no bounds, and who delight in shedding human blood, are angry when they kill people from whom they have received no injury, and who they themselves do not think have done them any injury; such as were Apollodorus or Phalaris. This is not anger, it is ferocity: for it does not do hurt because it has received injury: but is even willing to receive injury, provided it may do hurt. It does not long to inflict stripes and mangle bodies to avenge its wrongs, but for its own pleasure. What then are we to say? This evil takes its rise from anger; for anger, after it has by long use and indulgence made a man forget mercy, and driven all feelings of human fellowship from his mind, passes finally into cruelty. Such men therefore laugh, rejoice, enjoy themselves greatly, and are as unlike as possible in countenance to angry men, since cruelty is their relaxation.

plain_english: They say that when Hannibal saw a ditch full of human blood, he cried out, "What a beautiful sight!" How much more beautiful would he have thought it if it had filled a river or a lake? Why should we be surprised that you find this sight more charming than any other? You were born in bloodshed and raised among slaughter from childhood. Fortune will follow you and favor your cruelty for twenty years. It will show you everywhere the sight you love. You will see it at Trasimene and at Cannae, and finally at your own city of Carthage. Volesus, who not long ago served as governor of Asia Minor under Emperor Augustus, beheaded three hundred people in one day. Then he strutted around among the corpses with a proud look, as if he had done something grand and remarkable. He shouted in Greek, "What a kingly deed!" What would this man have done if he had actually been a king? This was not anger, but something worse and incurable.
original_excerpt: It is said that when Hannibal saw a trench full of human blood, he exclaimed, "O, what a beauteous sight!" How much more beautiful would he have thought it, if it had filled a river or a lake? Why should we wonder that you should be charmed with this sight above all others, you who were born in bloodshed and brought up amid slaughter from a child? Fortune will follow you and favour your cruelty for twenty years, and will display to you everywhere the sight that you love. You will behold it both at Trasumene and at Cannae, and lastly at your own city of Carthage. Volesus, who not long ago, under the Emperor Augustus, was proconsul of Asia Minor, after he had one day beheaded three hundred persons, strutted out among the corpses with a haughty air, as though he had performed some grand and notable exploit, and exclaimed in Greek, "What a kingly action!" What would this man have done, had he been really a king? This was not anger, but a greater and an incurable disease.

plain_english: Our opponent argues, "Virtue should be angry at what is base, just as she approves of what is honorable." What would we think if he said virtue should be both mean and great? Yet that's exactly what he means when he wants her to be raised and lowered. Joy at a good action is grand and glorious, while anger at another's sin is base and fits a narrow mind. Virtue will never imitate vice while trying to stop it. She considers anger itself deserving of punishment, since it is often even more criminal than the faults it gets angry about. To rejoice and be glad is virtue's proper and natural job. It is beneath her dignity to be angry, just as it is to mourn. Sorrow is anger's companion, and all anger ends in sorrow — either from regret or from failure. Second, if it's the wise man's job to be angry at sins, he will be angrier the greater they are, and will often be angry. This means the wise man will not only be angry but quick to anger. But if we don't believe that great and frequent anger can find any place in the wise man's mind, why shouldn't we free him from this passion entirely? There can be no limit if he ought to be angry in proportion to what every man does. He will either be unjust if he is equally angry at unequal crimes, or he will be the most quick-tempered of men if he blazes into wrath as often as crimes deserve his anger.
original_excerpt: “Virtue,” argues our adversary, “ought to be angry with what is base, just as she approves of what is honourable.” What should we think if he said that virtue ought to be both mean and great; yet this is what he means, when he wants her to be raised and lowered, because joy at a good action is grand and glorious, while anger at another’s sin is base and befits a narrow mind: and virtue will never be guilty of imitating vice while she is repressing it; she considers anger to deserve punishment for itself, since it often is even more criminal than the faults which which it is angry. To rejoice and be glad is the proper and natural function of virtue: it is as much beneath her dignity to be angry, as to mourn: now, sorrow is the companion of anger, and all anger ends in sorrow, either from remorse or from failure. Secondly, if it be the part of the wise man to be angry with sins, he will be more angry the greater they are, and will often be angry: from which it follows that the wise man will not only be angry but irascible. Yet if we do not believe that great and frequent anger can find any place in the wise man’s mind, why should we not set him altogether free from this passion? for there can be no limit, if he ought to be angry in proportion to what every man does: because he will either be unjust if he is equally angry at unequal crimes, or he will be the most irascible of men, if he blazes into wrath as often as crimes deserve his anger.

plain_english:
What could be more unworthy of a wise person than letting their emotions depend on how wicked other people are? If that were true, then even the great Socrates couldn't come home with the same calm expression he had when he left.

Besides, if it's the wise person's job to get angry at evil deeds and feel upset about crimes, then no one would be more miserable than the wise person. His whole life would be spent in anger and grief. When would he have a moment without seeing something worth condemning? Every time he leaves his house, he'd have to walk among criminals, misers, wastrels, and degenerates — and people who are proud to be that way. He couldn't look anywhere without seeing something that would shock him. He'd collapse from exhaustion if he got angry every time reason demanded it.

Look at all those thousands rushing to the courts at dawn. How shameful their cases are, and how much more shameful their lawyers! One person attacks his father's will when he should have tried to deserve it instead. Another accuses his own mother. A third comes to inform on someone for the very crime he himself is even more obviously guilty of. The judge is chosen to condemn people for doing what he himself has done. And the audience takes the wrong side, fooled by the smooth voice of some speaker.
original_excerpt: What, too, can be more unworthy of the wise man, than that his passions should depend upon the wickedness of others? If so, the great Socrates will no longer be able to return home with the same expression of countenance with which he set out. Moreover, if it be the duty of the wise man to be angry at base deeds, and to be excited and saddened at crimes, then is there nothing more unhappy than the wise man, for all his life will be spent in anger and grief. What moment will there be at which he will not see something deserving of blame? whenever he leaves his house, he will be obliged to walk among men who are criminals, misers, spendthrifts, profligates, and who are happy in being so: he can turn his eyes in no direction without their finding something to shock them. He will faint, if he demands anger from himself as often as reason calls for it. All these thousands who are hurrying to the law courts at break of day, how base are their causes, and how much baser their advocates? One impugns his father’s will, when he would have done better to deserve it; another appears as the accuser of his mother; a third comes to inform against a man for committing the very crime of which he himself is yet more notoriously guilty. The judge, too, is chosen to condemn men for doing what he himself has done, and the audience takes the wrong side, led astray by the fine voice of the pleader.

plain_english: Why should I give you specific examples? Just look around. When you see the Forum packed with crowds, the voting grounds swarming with people, or the great Circus where most of the population gathers at once — know this: there are as many vices as there are people. Among those you see dressed in peaceful clothes, there is no peace. For a small profit, any one of them will try to destroy another. No one can gain anything without someone else losing. They hate successful people and look down on the unfortunate. They barely tolerate the powerful while crushing the weak. They burn with different desires. They would wreck everything for a bit of pleasure or profit. They live like gladiators in training — fighting the same people they live with every day. It's like a society of wild animals, except animals are gentle with their own kind and don't bite members of their own species. But humans tear each other apart and devour one another. They differ from dumb animals in only this way: animals are tame with those who feed them, but human rage attacks the very people who raised them.
original_excerpt: Why need I dwell upon individual cases? Be assured, when you see the Forum crowded with a multitude, the Saepta[4] swarming with people, or the great Circus, in which the greater part of the people find room to show themselves at once, that among them there are as many vices as there are men. Among those whom you see in the garb of peace there is no peace: for a small profit any one of them will attempt the ruin of another: no one can gain anything save by another’s loss. They hate the fortunate and despise the unfortunate: they grudgingly endure the great, and oppress the small: they are fired by divers lusts: they would wreck everything for the sake of a little pleasure or plunder: they live as though they were in a school of gladiators, fighting with the same people with whom they live: it is like a society of wild beasts, save that beasts are tame with one another, and refrain from biting their own species, whereas men tear one another, and gorge themselves upon one another. They differ from dumb animals in this alone, that the latter are tame with those who feed them, whereas the rage of the former preys on those very persons by whom they were brought up.

plain_english: A wise man would never stop being angry once he started, because every place is packed with vice and crime. More evil happens than punishment can ever fix. People seem to be racing each other to see who can be most wicked. Each day brings more eagerness to sin and less shame. Throwing aside all respect for what is good and just, lust rushes wherever it wants to go. Crimes are no longer done in secret — they happen right in front of us. Wickedness has become so common and taken such deep root in everyone's hearts that innocence isn't just rare anymore. It no longer exists. Do people break the law one at a time, or just a few together? No, they rise up everywhere at once, as if responding to some universal signal, to erase the line between right and wrong.
original_excerpt: The wise man will never cease to be angry, if he once begins, so full is every place of vices and crimes. More evil is done than can be healed by punishment: men seem engaged in a vast race of wickedness. Every day there is greater eagerness to sin, less modesty. Throwing aside all reverence for what is better and more just, lust rushes whithersoever it thinks fit, and crimes are no longer committed by stealth, they take place before our eyes, and wickedness has become so general and gained such a footing in everyone's breast that innocence is no longer rare, but no longer exists. Do men break the law singly, or a few at a time? Nay, they rise in all quarters at once, as though obeying some universal signal, to wipe out the boundaries of right and wrong.

plain_english: "No guest is safe from his host. No father-in-law is safe from his son-in-law. Brothers rarely love each other. Wives want to destroy their husbands. Husbands want to kill their wives. Stepmothers prepare deadly poison. Children wonder when their fathers will finally die." But these crimes are nothing! The poet hasn't described a whole nation split into two enemy camps. He hasn't described parents and children fighting on opposite sides. He hasn't described Rome set on fire by Romans themselves. He hasn't described cavalry troops hunting down the condemned. He hasn't described wells poisoned, plagues created by human hands, children digging trenches around their own besieged parents. He hasn't described packed prisons, cities burned to the ground, dark tyrannies, secret plots to overthrow governments and destroy peoples. He hasn't described men celebrating acts that used to be called crimes — rape, corruption, and lust. Add to this list: nations breaking their word, broken treaties, the strong stealing everything the weak cannot defend, cheating, theft, fraud, and debt dodging so widespread that three courts couldn't handle it all. If you want the wise man to get as angry as human crimes deserve, he wouldn't just be angry. He'd go completely insane with rage.
original_excerpt: "Host is not safe from guest, Father-in-law from son; but seldom love Exists 'twixt brothers; wives long to destroy Their husbands, husbands long to slay their wives, Stepmothers deadly aconite prepare And child-heirs wonder when their sires will die." And how small a part of men's crimes are these! The poet[5] has not described one people divided into two hostile camps, parents and children enrolled on opposite sides, Rome set on fire by the hand of a Roman, troops of fierce horsemen scouring the country to track out the hiding-places of the proscribed, wells defiled with poison, plagues created by human hands, trenches dug by children round their beleaguered parents, crowded prisons, conflagrations that consume whole cities, gloomy tyrannies, secret plots to establish despotisms and ruin peoples, and men glorying in those deeds which, as long as it was possible to repress them, were counted as crimes—I mean rape, debauchery, and lust . . . . . Add to these, public acts of national bad faith, broken treaties, everything that cannot defend itself carried off as plunder by the stronger, knaveries, thefts, frauds, and disownings of debt such as three of our present law-courts would not suffice to deal with. If you want the wise man to be as angry as the atrocity of men's crimes requires, he must not merely be angry, but must go mad with rage.

plain_english: You should think we shouldn't get angry at people's flaws. What would you say about someone who gets mad at people stumbling in the dark? Or at deaf people who can't hear orders? Or at children who forget their duties and get caught up in games and silly jokes with friends? What if you choose to get angry at sick people for being sick, at old people for aging, or at tired people for being tired? Among all the bad things about humanity is this: our minds are confused. We not only can't help making mistakes — we actually love making mistakes. To avoid getting angry at individuals, you have to forgive everyone. You have to grant forgiveness to the entire human race. If you get angry at young and old people for doing wrong, you'll have to be angry at babies too. After all, they'll do wrong soon enough.
original_excerpt: You will rather think that we should not be angry with people's faults; for what shall we say of one who is angry with those who stumble in the dark, or with deaf people who cannot hear his orders, or with children, because they forget their duty and interest themselves in the games and silly jokes of their companions? What shall we say if you choose to be angry with weaklings for being sick, for growing old, or becoming fatigued? Among the other misfortunes of humanity is this, that men's intellects are confused, and they not only cannot help going wrong, but love to go wrong. To avoid being angry with individuals, you must pardon the whole mass, you must grant forgiveness to the entire human race. If you are angry with young and old men because they do wrong, you will be angry with infants also, for they soon will do wrong.

plain_english: Do you get angry with children who are too young to understand right from wrong? Of course not. But being human is an even better excuse than being a child. We're all born with minds that can go wrong just like our bodies can get sick. We're not stupid or slow — we're actually too clever for our own good. We use our intelligence badly and lead each other astray by our example. If someone follows others who started down the wrong path first, you can hardly blame them for getting lost. A general might punish one deserter harshly, but if the whole army deserts, he has to forgive them all. What stops a wise person from getting angry? The sheer number of people doing wrong. He sees how unfair and dangerous it is to rage against faults that we all share.
original_excerpt: Does any one become angry with children, who are too young to comprehend distinctions? Yet, to be a human being is a greater and a better excuse than to be a child. Thus are we born, as creatures liable to as many disorders of the mind as of the body; not dull and slow-witted, but making a bad use of our keenness of wit, and leading one another into vice by our example. He who follows others who have started before him on the wrong road is surely excusable for having wandered on[6] the highway. A general's severity may be shown in the case of individual deserters; but where a whole army deserts, it must needs be pardoned. What is it that puts a stop to the wise man's anger? It is the number of sinners. He perceives how unjust and how dangerous it is to be angry with vices which all men share.

plain_english: Heraclitus used to cry whenever he went outside and saw so many people living miserable lives — or really, dying miserable deaths. He felt sorry for everyone he met who seemed happy and cheerful. He had a gentle heart, but it was too tender for his own good. In fact, he was one of the people he should have been crying for. Democritus was the opposite. He supposedly never appeared in public without laughing. Human affairs struck him as so ridiculous that he couldn't take any of them seriously. So where does that leave room for anger? Everything should either make us laugh or make us cry. A wise person won't get angry at people who do wrong. Why not? Because he knows that nobody is born wise — we have to become wise. He knows that very few people in any generation actually become wise. He understands what human life is really like. No reasonable person gets angry at nature. What would you say about someone who was shocked that fruit trees don't grow wild in the forest? Or someone amazed that thornbushes don't produce useful berries?
original_excerpt: Heraclitcus, whenever he came out of doors and beheld around him such a number of men who were living wretchedly, nay, rather perishing wretchedly, used to weep: he pitied all those who met him joyous and happy. He was of a gentle but too weak disposition; and he himself was one of those for whom he ought to have wept. Democritus, on the other hand, is said never to have appeared in public without laughing; so little did men's serious occupations appear serious to him. What room is there for anger? Everything ought either to move us to tears or to laughter. The wise man will not be angry with sinners. Why not? Because he knows that no one is born wise, but becomes so: he knows that very few wise men are produced in any age, because he thoroughly understands the circumstances of human life. Now, no sane man is angry with nature: for what should we say if a man chose to be surprised that fruit did not hang on the thickets of a forest, or to wonder at bushes and thorns not being covered with some useful berry?

plain_english: No one gets angry at nature for causing a birth defect. The wise person stays calm and deals honestly with mistakes. He's not an enemy of wrongdoers — he helps them improve. Every day he goes out thinking: "I'll meet many people today who drink too much, who chase sex, who are ungrateful, greedy, and driven mad by ambition." He looks at all of them as kindly as a doctor looks at his patients. When a ship is leaking badly through cracked boards, does the captain get angry at the sailors or the ship? No. Instead, he tries to fix it. He blocks some leaks, bails out water, plugs every hole he can see. He works constantly to fight the hidden leaks that keep flooding the ship. He doesn't give up just because water pours in as fast as he pumps it out. We need a long, steady fight against permanent and endless problems. Not to defeat them completely, but just to keep them from overwhelming us.
original_excerpt: No one is angry when nature excuses a defect. The wise man, therefore, being tranquil, and dealing candidly with mistakes, not an enemy to but an improver of sinners, will go abroad every day in the following frame of mind:—"Many men will meet me who are drunkards, lustful, ungrateful, greedy, and excited by the frenzy of ambition." He will view all these as benignly as a physician does his patients. When a man's ship leaks freely through its opened seams, does he become angry with the sailors or the ship itself? No; instead of that, he tries to remedy it: he shuts out some water, bales out some other, closes all the holes that he can see, and by ceaseless labour counteracts those which are out of sight and which let water into the hold; nor does he relax his efforts because as much water as he pumps out runs in again. We need a long-breathed struggle against permanent and prolific evils; not, indeed, to quell them, but merely to prevent their overpowering us.

plain_english: "Anger is useful," our opponent says, "because it prevents contempt and frightens bad people." But here's the problem with this argument. First, if anger is powerful because it threatens people, then it's also hateful for the same reason it's scary. And being hated is more dangerous than being looked down on. Second, if anger is weak, it becomes even more contemptible and ridiculous. What's more pathetic than anger that just turns into meaningless ranting? Just because something is frightening doesn't make it good. Wisdom doesn't want people to say about a wise person what they say about a wild animal — that fear is his weapon. We fear fever, gout, and painful sores, but does that make them good? Of course not. We despise these things and think they're disgusting and shameful, which is exactly why we fear them. Anger works the same way. It's ugly and shouldn't be feared, yet many people do fear it — just like children fear a scary mask.
original_excerpt: "Anger," says our opponent, "is useful, because it avoids contempt, and because it frightens bad men." Now, in the first place, if anger is strong in proportion to its threats, it is hateful for the same reason that it is terrible: and it is more dangerous to be hated than to be despised. If, again, it is without strength, it is much more exposed to contempt, and cannot avoid ridicule; for what is more flat than anger when it breaks out into meaningless ravings? Moreover, because some things are somewhat terrible, they are not on that account desirable: nor does wisdom wish it to be said of the wise man, as it is of a wild beast, that the fear which he inspires is as a weapon to him. Why, do we not fear fever, gout, consuming ulcers? and is there, for that reason, any good in them? nay; on the other hand, they are all despised and thought to be foul and base, and are for this very reason feared. So, too, anger is in itself hideous and by no means to be feared; yet it is feared by many, just as a hideous mask is feared by children.

plain_english: How can we explain this fact: terror always comes back to haunt whoever creates it. No one who lives in peace is truly feared. Here you should remember that line from Laberius. When it was spoken in the theater during the civil war, the whole audience loved it because it captured how everyone felt: "He must fear many, whom so many fear." This is how nature works. Whatever grows powerful by making others afraid cannot escape fear itself. See how lions jump at the smallest sounds! How the fiercest animals get spooked by unfamiliar shadows, voices, or smells! Whatever terrorizes others lives in terror too. So no wise person should want to be feared. And don't think anger is something great just because it scares people. Even the most worthless things can be frightening — like poisonous bugs whose bite can kill you. A string decorated with feathers can stop entire herds of wild animals and guide them into traps. That's why they call it a "Scarer." Stupid creatures get scared by stupid things. The sound of chariots and sight of spinning wheels drives lions back into their cages. Elephants run from squealing pigs. We fear anger the same way children fear the dark or wild beasts fear red feathers. Anger has nothing solid or brave about it. It only works on weak minds.
original_excerpt:
How can we answer the fact that terror always works back to him who inspired it, and that no one is feared who is himself at peace? At this point it is well that you should remember that verse of Laberius, which, when pronounced in the theatre during the height of the civil war, caught the fancy of the whole people as though it expressed the national feeling:—

"He must fear many, whom so many fear."

Thus has nature ordained, that whatever becomes great by causing fear to others is not free from fear itself. How disturbed lions are at the faintest noises! How excited those fiercest of beasts become at strange shadows, voices, or smells! Whatever is a terror to others, fears for itself. There can be no reason, therefore, for any wise man to wish to be feared, and no one need think that anger is anything great because it strikes terror, since even the most despicable things are feared, as, for example, noxious vermin whose bite is venomous: and since a string set with feathers stops the largest herds of wild beasts and guides them into traps, it is no wonder that from its effect it should be named a "Scarer."[7] Foolish creatures are frightened by foolish things: the movement of chariots and the sight of their wheels turning round drives lions back into their cage: elephants are frightened at the cries of pigs: and so also we fear anger just as children fear the dark, or wild beasts fear red feathers: it has in itself nothing solid or valiant, but it affects feeble minds.

plain_english: "Evil must be removed from the natural order," says our opponent, "if you want to remove anger. And neither of these things can be done." First, a person can avoid being cold even when it's winter by nature's calendar. They can avoid being hot even when it's summer by the almanac. They might live in a sheltered place, or they might have trained their body to handle extremes so well that they don't feel heat or cold. Now flip this argument around: You must remove anger from your mind before you can let virtue in. Vices and virtues cannot mix. No one can be both angry and good at the same time, any more than someone can be both sick and healthy.
original_excerpt: "Wickedness," says our adversary, "must be removed from the system of nature, if you wish to remove anger: neither of which things can be done." In the first place, it is possible for a man not to be cold, although according to the system of nature it may be winter-time, nor yet to suffer from heat, although it be summer according to the almanac. He may be protected against the inclement time of the year by dwelling in a favoured spot, or he may have so trained his body to endurance that it feels neither heat nor cold. Next, reverse this saying:—You must remove anger from your mind before you can take virtue into the same, because vices and virtues cannot combine, and none can at the same time be both an angry man and a good man, any more than he can be both sick and well.

plain_english: "You can't completely remove anger from the mind," some people say. "Human nature won't allow it." But there's nothing so hard that the human mind can't overcome it. With constant practice, we can master anything. No passion is so wild that discipline can't tame it. The mind can do whatever it commands itself to do. Some people have succeeded in never smiling. Others have given up wine, sex, or even all drinks. Some people who need little sleep have learned to stay awake for long periods without getting tired. People have learned to run on thin ropes, even when they're slanted. They carry huge weights that seem beyond human strength. They dive to incredible depths and hold their breath underwater for impossibly long times.
original_excerpt: "It is not possible," says he, "to remove anger altogether from the mind, nor does human nature admit of it." Yet there is nothing so hard and difficult that the mind of man cannot overcome it, and with which unremitting study will not render him familiar, nor are there any passions so fierce and independent that they cannot be tamed by discipline. The mind can carry out whatever orders it gives itself: some have succeeded in never smiling: some have forbidden themselves wine, sexual intercourse, or even drink of all kinds. Some, who are satisfied with short hours of rest, have learned to watch for long periods without weariness. Men have learned to run upon the thinnest ropes even when slanting, to carry huge burdens, scarcely within the compass of human strength, or to dive to enormous depths and suffer themselves to remain under the sea without any chance of drawing breath.

plain_english: There are countless other examples where practice has overcome every obstacle. They prove that nothing is too hard if your mind is set on enduring it. The men I just mentioned get either no reward or one that hardly matches their endless effort. What great thing does someone gain by learning to walk on a tightrope? Or by carrying heavy weights on their shoulders? Or by staying awake for days? Or by diving to the bottom of the sea? Yet their patient work makes all these things possible — for almost nothing in return. So shouldn't we use that same patience when such a prize awaits us: the unbroken calm of a happy life? What a blessing it would be to escape from anger, the worst of all evils, and along with it from frenzy, cruelty, and madness — all its companions.
original_excerpt: There are a thousand other instances in which application has conquered all obstacles, and proved that nothing which the mind has set itself to endure is difficult. The men whom I have just mentioned gain either no reward or one that is unworthy of their unwearied application; for what great thing does a man gain by applying his intellect to walking upon a tight rope? or to placing great burdens upon his shoulders? or to keeping sleep from his eyes? or to reaching the bottom of the sea? and yet their patient labour brings all these things to pass for a trifling reward. Shall not we then call in the aid of patience, we whom such a prize awaits, the unbroken calm of a happy life? How great a blessing is it to escape from anger, that chief of all evils, and therewith from frenzy, ferocity, cruelty, and madness, its attendants?

plain_english: There's no point in defending anger or making excuses for it. Don't tell me it's useful or unavoidable. Every vice has its defenders — that doesn't make anger something we can't overcome. The problems we face can be fixed. We were born with a natural pull toward good, and nature will help us if we actually try to improve. The path to virtue isn't steep and rough like some people think. You can reach it on level ground. I'm telling you the truth here: the road to happiness is easy. You just need to start walking it with some luck and divine help. What you're doing now is much harder work. What's more peaceful than a calm mind? What's more exhausting than anger? What's more relaxed than mercy? What's busier than cruelty? Good behavior takes a holiday while vice works overtime. Bottom line: any virtue is easy to develop, but vices cost you dearly. We need to remove anger from our minds completely. Even people who say we should just keep it under control are admitting this partly. Get rid of it entirely — there's nothing good it does for you. Without anger, we can stop crime more easily and fairly. We can punish bad people and help them change. A wise person will do what's right without any evil passion helping him. He won't use tools that need constant watching to keep them from spinning out of control.
original_excerpt: There is no reason why we should seek to defend such a passion as this or excuse its excesses by declaring it to be either useful or unavoidable. What vice, indeed, is without its defenders? yet this is no reason why you should declare anger to be ineradicable. The evils from which we suffer are curable, and since we were born with a natural bias towards good, nature herself will help us if we try to amend our lives. Nor is the path to virtue steep and rough, as some think it to be: it may be reached on level ground. This is no untrue tale which I come to tell you: the road to happiness is easy; do you only enter upon it with good luck and the good help of the gods themselves. It is much harder to do what you are doing. What is more restful than a mind at peace, and what more toilsome than anger? What is more at leisure than clemency, what fuller of business than cruelty? Modesty keeps holiday while vice is overwhelmed with work. In fine, the culture of any of the virtues is easy, while vices require a great expense. Anger ought to be removed from our minds: even those who say that it ought to be kept low admit this to some extent: let it be got rid of altogether; there is nothing to be gained by it. Without it we can more easily and more justly put an end to crime, punish bad men, and amend their lives. The wise man will do his duty in all things without the help of any evil passion, and will use no auxiliaries which require watching narrowly lest they get beyond his control.

plain_english: Anger should never become a habit. But sometimes we can pretend to be angry when we need to wake up people who aren't paying attention — like using spurs and torches to get lazy horses moving. Sometimes we need to use fear on people who won't listen to reason. But actually being angry is as useless as grieving or being afraid. "But don't some situations naturally make us angry?" Yes — and those are exactly the times we most need to control our rage. It's not that hard to master our emotions. Athletes focus on the crudest parts of training, yet they can take punches and pain to wear down their opponent. They don't strike when anger tells them to, but when the right moment comes. Pyrrhus, the most famous athletic trainer, always told his students not to lose their tempers. Anger ruins technique and only thinks about causing harm. Reason often tells us to wait, while anger demands revenge. People who might have survived their first troubles get hit with worse ones. Some have been exiled because they couldn't stand a single insult. Others have fallen into deep misery because they wouldn't quietly endure the smallest slight. They've brought slavery upon themselves because they were too proud to give up even a tiny bit of their freedom.
original_excerpt: Anger, then, must never become a habit with us, but we may sometimes affect to be angry when we wish to rouse up the dull minds of those whom we address, just as we rouse up horses who are slow at starting with goads and firebrands. We must sometimes apply fear to persons upon whom reason makes no impression: yet to be angry is of no more use than to grieve or to be afraid. “What? do not circumstances arise which provoke us to anger?” Yes: but at those times above all others we ought to choke down our wrath. Nor is it difficult to conquer our spirit, seeing that athletes, who devote their whole attention to the basest parts of themselves, nevertheless are able to endure blows and pain, in order to exhaust the strength of the striker, and do not strike when anger bids them, but when opportunity invites them. It is said that Pyrrhus, the most celebrated trainer for gymnastic contests, used habitually to impress upon his pupils not to lose their tempers: for anger spoils their science, and thinks only how it can hurt: so that often reason counsels patience while anger counsels revenge, and we, who might have survived our first misfortunes, are exposed to worse ones. Some have been driven into exile by their impatience of a single contemptuous word, have been plunged into the deepest miseries because they would not endure the most trifling wrong in silence, and have brought upon themselves the yoke of slavery because they were too proud to give up the least part of their entire liberty.

plain_english: "To prove that anger has something noble about it," our opponent says, "just look at free nations like the Germans and Scythians. They're especially quick to anger." But here's why that happens: bold and daring minds are prone to anger before they learn discipline. Some emotions only take root in better types of people — just like good land, even when it's wild, grows strong weeds and tall trees in rich soil. In the same way, naturally bold personalities create irritability. Being hot and fiery, they have nothing weak or petty about them. But their energy goes in the wrong direction. This happens to everyone who rises by natural talent alone without training. Unless these minds are controlled, they fall from courage into reckless, dangerous habits. "But aren't gentler spirits connected to gentler vices, like being too soft-hearted, too loving, or too shy?" Yes — and that's why I can often spot a good nature by its very flaws. But just because these flaws prove someone has a superior nature doesn't mean they're not still vices. Besides, all those nations that are free because they're wild — like lions or wolves — can't command any more than they can obey. Their mental strength isn't civilized but fierce and uncontrollable. And no one can rule unless they can also be ruled. So the world's great empires have almost always stayed in the hands of nations with milder climates. Those who live near the frozen north have uncivilized tempers — "just like their native skies," as the poet says.
original_excerpt:
“That you may be sure,” says our opponent, “that anger has in it something noble, pray look at the free nations, such as the Germans and Scythians, who are especially prone to anger.” The reason of this is that stout and daring intellects are liable to anger before they are tamed by discipline; for some passions engraft themselves upon the better class of dispositions only, just as good land, even when waste, grows strong brushwood, and the trees are tall which stand upon a fertile soil. In like manner, dispositions which are naturally bold produce irritability, and, being hot and fiery, have no mean or trivial qualities, but their energy is misdirected, as happens with all those who without training come to the front by their natural advantages alone, whose minds, unless they be brought under control, degenerate from a courageous temper into habits of rashness and reckless daring. “What? are not milder spirits linked with gentler vices, such as tenderness of heart, love, and bashfulness?” Yes, and therefore I can often point out to you a good disposition by its own faults: yet their being the proofs of a superior nature does not prevent their being vices. Moreover, all those nations which are free because they are wild, like lions or wolves, cannot command any more than they can obey: for the strength of their intellect is not civilized, but fierce and unmanageable: now, no one is able to rule unless he is also able to be ruled. Consequently, the empire of the world has almost always remained in the hands of those nations who enjoy a milder climate. Those who dwell near the frozen north have uncivilized tempers—

“Just on the model of their native skies,”

as the poet has it.

plain_english: My opponent argues that the most noble animals are those with great capacity for anger. He's wrong to hold up creatures who act on impulse rather than reason as examples for humans to follow. In humans, reason replaces impulse. Even with animals, not all benefit from the same traits. Anger helps lions, timidity helps deer, boldness helps hawks, and flight helps doves. But I'll go further — it's not even true that the best animals are the angriest. Wild beasts that hunt for food might be better when they're angry, but I'd praise patient oxen and horses who obey the reins. Why would you point humans toward such poor examples when you have the universe and God as models? Humans alone can imitate God because we alone understand Him. "The most hot-tempered people," my opponent says, "are thought to be the most honest." Sure — compared to cheats and con artists, they seem simple because they speak their minds. I wouldn't call such people simple, just careless. We use the word "simple" for all kinds of fools — gluttons, spendthrifts, and people whose vices are obvious.
original_excerpt: Those animals, urges our opponent, are held to be the most generous who have large capacity for anger. He is mistaken when he holds up creatures who act from impulse instead of reason as patterns for men to follow, because in man reason takes the place of impulse. Yet even with animals, all do not alike profit by the same thing. Anger is of use to lions, timidity to stags, boldness to hawks, flight to doves. What if I declare that it is not even true that the best animals are the most prone to anger? I may suppose that wild beasts, who gain their food by rapine, are better the angrier they are; but I should praise oxen and horses who obey the rein for their patience. What reason, however, have you for referring mankind to such wretched models, when you have the universe and God, whom he alone of animals imitates because he alone comprehends Him? “The most irritable men,” says he, “are thought to be the most straightforward of all.” Yes, because they are compared with swindlers and sharpers, and appear to be simple because they are outspoken. I should not call such men simple, but heedless. We give this title of “simple” to all fools, gluttons, spendthrifts, and men whose vices lie on the surface.

plain_english: "An orator speaks better when he's angry," our opponent says. Not true. He speaks better when he pretends to be angry. Actors bring down the house with their performances — not when they're actually angry, but when they act anger well. It's the same when addressing a jury or crowd. When you need to influence people, you must pretend to feel anger, fear, or pity before you can make others feel them. Often the pretense of passion works better than real passion ever could. "A mind that doesn't feel anger is weak," he says. True — if it has nothing stronger than anger to rely on. A person should be neither robber nor victim, neither soft-hearted nor cruel. The first comes from a too-weak mind, the second from a too-hard one. Let the wise person be moderate. When action is needed, let him use force — not anger.
original_excerpt: “An orator,” says our opponent, “sometimes speaks better, when he is angry.” Not so, but when he pretends to be angry: for so also actors bring down the house by their playing, not when they are really angry, but when they act the angry man well: and in like manner, in addressing a jury or a popular assembly, or in any other position in which the minds of others have to be influenced at our pleasure, we must ourselves pretend to feel anger, fear, or pity before we can make others feel them, and often the pretence of passion will do what the passion itself could not have done. “The mind which does not feel anger,” says he, “is feeble.” True, if it has nothing stronger than anger to support it. A man ought to be neither robber nor victim, neither tender-hearted nor cruel. The former belongs to an over-weak mind, the latter to an over-hard one. Let the wise man be moderate, and when things have to be done somewhat briskly, let him call force, not anger, to his aid.

plain_english:
Now that we've talked about the nature of anger, let's move on to its remedies. I think there are two kinds: one to prevent us from getting angry in the first place, and another to prevent us from doing harm once we're already angry. Just like we follow one set of health rules to stay well and different rules to recover when we're sick, we need different approaches to ward off anger and to calm it down. To avoid anger altogether, we need certain general principles that apply to everyone's life. We can divide these into lessons for educating the young and guidelines for adult life.

Education should be handled with the greatest care and persistence. It's easy to shape minds while they're still soft, but it's hard to tear out bad habits that have grown up with us.
original_excerpt:
Now that we have discussed the questions propounded concerning anger, let us pass on to the consideration of its remedies. These, I imagine, are two-fold: the one class preventing our becoming angry, the other preventing our doing wrong when we are angry. As with the body we adopt a certain regimen to keep ourselves in health, and use different rules to bring back health when lost, so likewise we must repel anger in one fashion and quench it in another. That we may avoid it, certain general rules of conduct which apply to all men’s lives must be impressed upon us. We may divide these into such as are of use during the education of the young and in after-life.

Education ought to be carried on with the greatest and most salutary assiduity: for it is easy to mould minds while they are still tender, but it is difficult to uproot vices which have grown up with ourselves.

plain_english: A hot temperament is naturally most prone to anger. Just as there are four elements — fire, air, earth, and water — there are four corresponding qualities: hot, cold, dry, and moist. The way these elements mix determines the differences between lands, animals, bodies, and personalities. Our dispositions lean toward whichever element is strongest in us. This is why we call some regions wet or dry, warm or cold. The same applies to animals and people. It makes a huge difference how much moisture or heat a person contains. Their character will reflect whichever element dominates them.
original_excerpt: A hot mind is naturally the most prone to anger: for as there are four elements,[8] consisting of fire, air, earth, and water, so there are powers corresponding and equivalent to each of these, namely, hot, cold, dry, and moist. Now the mixture of the elements is the cause of the diversities of lands and of animals, of bodies and of character, and our dispositions incline to one or the other of these according as the strength of each element prevails in us. Hence it is that we call some regions wet or dry, warm or cold. The same distinctions apply likewise to animals and mankind; it makes a great difference how much moisture or heat a man contains; his character will partake of whichever element has the largest share in him.

plain_english:
People with hot temperaments get angry easily. Fire is full of movement and energy. Cold makes people cowardly, because cold is slow and stiff. Some of our Stoic philosophers think anger happens when blood boils around the heart. They say this is why we feel anger in our chest — because the chest is the warmest part of the body.

People with more moisture in them get angry slowly. They don't have heat ready to go, so they need movement to build it up. That's why women and children have sharp anger rather than strong anger. It flares up over small things.

In the dry times of life, anger is violent and powerful. But it doesn't grow much, because as heat fades, cold takes over. Old people are cranky and complain a lot. So do sick people and those recovering from illness. Anyone whose heat has been drained by exhaustion or blood loss acts this way.

People wasted by thirst or hunger are the same. So are those who are naturally pale and weak from poor diet. Wine sparks anger because it increases heat. Depending on the person, some explode when very drunk, others when just slightly drunk. This is also why blonde, red-faced people are so passionate. They naturally have the color that others turn when angry. Their blood is hot and easily stirred up.
original_excerpt: A warm temper of mind will make men prone to anger; for fire is full of movement and vigour; a mixture of coldness makes men cowards, for cold is sluggish and contracted. Because of this, some of our Stoics think that anger is excited in our breasts by the boiling of the blood round the heart: indeed, that place is assigned to anger for no other reason than because the breast is the warmest part of the whole body. Those who have more moisture in them become angry by slow degrees, because they have no heat ready at hand, but it has to be obtained by movement; wherefore the anger of women and children is sharp rather than strong, and arises on lighter provocation. At dry times of life anger is violent and powerful, yet without increase, and adding little to itself, because as heat dies away cold takes its place. Old men are testy and full of complaints, as also are sick people and convalescents, and all whose store of heat has been consumed by weariness or loss of blood. Those who are wasted by thirst or hunger are in the same condition, as also are those whose frame is naturally bloodless and faints from want of generous diet. Wine kindles anger, because it increases heat; according to each man's disposition, some fly into a passion when they are heavily drunk, some when they are slightly drunk: nor is there any other reason than this why yellow-haired, ruddy-complexioned people should be excessively passionate, seeing that they are naturally of the colour which others put on during anger; for their blood is hot and easily set in motion.

plain_english: Just as nature makes some people naturally angry, many other things can do the same damage. Some people become angry from illness or injury. Others from overwork, sleepless nights, worry, passionate desires, and love. Anything that hurts the body or mind makes a troubled person more likely to complain. But these are just the triggers and causes of anger. Your mental habits have enormous power. If your habits are harsh, they make the problem worse. As for your nature — that's hard to change. We can't alter the mix of elements we were born with. But knowledge helps this much: we should keep wine away from hot-tempered people. Plato thought boys shouldn't drink either, so we don't add fire to fire.
original_excerpt: But just as nature makes some men prone to anger, so there are many other causes which have the same power as nature. Some are brought into this condition by disease or bodily injury, others by hard work, long watching, nights of anxiety, ardent longings, and love: and everything else which is hurtful to the body or the spirit inclines the distempered mind to find fault. All these, however, are but the beginning and causes of anger. Habit of mind has very great power, and, if it be harsh, increases the disorder. As for nature, it is difficult to alter it, nor may we change the mixture of the elements which was formed once for all at our birth: yet knowledge will be so far of service, that we should keep wine out of the reach of hot-tempered men, which Plato thinks ought also to be forbidden to boys, so that fire be not made fiercer.

plain_english: Don't overfeed these men either. If you do, their bodies will get bigger, and their minds will get bigger with them. Such men should exercise, but not to the point of exhaustion. This will cool down their natural heat without draining it completely. It will also work off their excess fiery energy. Games will help too. Moderate pleasure calms the mind and brings it into balance. People with temperaments that lean toward moisture, dryness, or stiffness don't risk anger. But they do risk worse vices — cowardice, gloominess, despair, and suspicion. These types need to be softened, comforted, and cheered up. We need different remedies for anger versus sullenness. These two vices need not just different treatments, but completely opposite ones. So let's always attack whichever vice is winning.
original_excerpt: Neither should such men be over-fed: for if so, their bodies will swell, and their minds will swell with them. Such men ought to take exercise, stopping short, however, of fatigue, in order that their natural heat may be abated, but not exhausted, and their excess of fiery spirit may be worked off. Games also will be useful: for moderate pleasure relieves the mind and brings it to a proper balance. With those temperaments which incline to moisture, or dryness and stiffness, there is no danger of anger, but there is fear of greater vices, such as cowardice, moroseness, despair, and suspiciousness: such dispositions therefore ought to be softened, comforted, and restored to cheerfulness: and since we must make use of different remedies for anger and for sullenness, and these two vices require not only unlike, but absolutely opposite modes of treatment, let us always attack that one of them which is gaining the mastery.

plain_english: I promise you, it's incredibly important that boys get a solid upbringing. But managing their education is tricky. We need to be careful not to encourage anger in them, while also not crushing their spirit. This requires constant attention. The qualities we want to build up and the ones we want to control are often fed by the same things. Even when you're watching closely, you can be fooled by how similar they look. A boy's spirit grows when he has freedom and shrinks when he's treated like a slave. He rises when praised and starts to expect great things from himself. But this same treatment can also create arrogance and a quick temper. So we have to guide him between these two extremes — sometimes holding him back, sometimes pushing him forward.
original_excerpt: It is, I assure you, of the greatest service to boys that they should be soundly brought up, yet to regulate their education is difficult, because it is our duty to be careful neither to cherish a habit of anger in them, nor to blunt the edge of their spirit. This needs careful watching, for both qualities, both those which are to be encouraged, and those which are to be checked, are fed by the same things; and even a careful watcher may be deceived by their likeness. A boy's spirit is increased by freedom and depressed by slavery: it rises when praised, and is led to conceive great expectations of itself: yet this same treatment produces arrogance and quickness of temper: we must therefore guide him between these two extremes, using the curb at one time and the spur at another.

plain_english: He should never have to put up with harsh or humiliating treatment. He should never have to beg pathetically for anything, and he shouldn't get things by begging. Instead, let him earn things because of who he is, his past good behavior, or his promises to do better in the future. When he competes with other children, don't let him sulk or lose his temper. Make sure he stays on good terms with his competitors. That way, during the contest itself, he learns to want victory — not to hurt his opponent. When he wins or does something worth praising, let him enjoy his success. But don't let him get carried away with excitement. Joy leads to showing off, and showing off leads to arrogance and thinking too highly of yourself. Give him some downtime, but don't let him become lazy and idle. Keep him far away from luxury. Nothing makes children more likely to get angry than soft, spoiled upbringing. The more you pamper an only child, and the more freedom you give orphans, the more you ruin them.
original_excerpt: He must undergo no servile or degrading treatment; he never must beg abjectly for anything, nor must he gain anything by begging; let him rather receive it for his own sake, for his past good behaviour, or for his promises of future good conduct. In contests with his comrades we ought not to allow him to become sulky or fly into a passion: let us see that he be on friendly terms with those whom he contends with, so that in the struggle itself he may learn to wish not to hurt his antagonist but to conquer him: whenever he has gained the day or done something praiseworthy, we should allow him to enjoy his victory, but not to rush into transports of delight: for joy leads to exultation, and exultation leads to swaggering and excessive self-esteem, We ought to allow him some relaxation, yet not yield him up to laziness and sloth, and we ought to keep him far beyond the reach of luxury, for nothing makes children more prone to anger than a soft and fond bringing-up, so that the more only children are indulged, and the more liberty is given to orphans, the more they are corrupted.

plain_english: A child who is never told "no" won't be able to handle rejection when he grows up. His worried mother always dries his tears. His tutor gets punished for the child's mistakes. Haven't you noticed how people get angrier as they gain more power? This is especially true for the rich, the well-born, and those in high positions. When success fills their sails, it stirs up all the most shallow and petty emotions in their minds. Success feeds anger. A person's proud ears get surrounded by crowds of flatterers who say things like: "How dare he talk to you that way! You're not acting with proper dignity! You're lowering yourself!" And so on, with all the words that even healthy, well-principled minds can barely resist. So keep flattery far away from children. Let a child hear the truth, and sometimes be afraid of it. Let him always respect it. Let him stand up when his elders enter the room.
original_excerpt: He to whom nothing is ever denied, will not be able to endure a rebuff, whose anxious mother always wipes away his tears, whose _paedagogus_[9] is made to pay for his shortcomings. Do you not observe how a man's anger becomes more violent as he rises in station? This shows itself especially in those that are rich and noble, or in great place, when the favouring gale has roused all the most empty and trivial passions of their minds. Prosperity fosters anger, when a man's proud ears are surrounded by a mob of flatterers, saying, "That man answer you! you do not act according to your dignity, you lower yourself." And so forth, with all the language which can hardly be resisted even by healthy and originally well-principled minds. Flattery, then, must be kept well out of the way of children. Let a child hear the truth, and sometimes fear it: let him always reverence it. Let him rise in the presence of his elders.

plain_english: Don't give him what he wants when he throws a tantrum. Give it to him when he's calm and asks nicely. Let him see his father's wealth but not use it freely. Correct him when he does wrong. It helps to give boys teachers and tutors who stay calm and even-tempered. Children are like soft clay — they stick to whatever is nearby and take that shape. Young people copy the habits of their nurses and tutors. Once, a boy raised in Plato's house went home to his parents. When he saw his father shouting angrily, he said, "I never saw anyone at Plato's house act like that." I'm sure he learned to copy his father faster than he learned to copy Plato. Most importantly, keep his food simple, his clothes inexpensive, and the same style as his friends wear. If you start by putting him on equal footing with others, he won't get angry when someone compares him to them.
original_excerpt: Let him obtain nothing by flying into a passion: let him be given when he is quiet what was refused him when he cried for it: let him behold, but not make use of his father's wealth: let him be reproved for what he does wrong. It will be advantageous to furnish boys with even-tempered teachers and _paedagogi_: what is soft and unformed clings to what is near, and takes its shape: the habits of young men reproduce those of their nurses and _paedagogi_. Once, a boy who was brought up in Plato's house went home to his parents, and, on seeing his father shouting with passion, said, "I never saw any one at Plato's house act like that." I doubt not that he learned to imitate his father sooner than he learned to imitate Plato. Above all, let his food be scanty, his dress not costly, and of the same fashion as that of his comrades: if you begin by putting him on a level with many others, he will not be angry when some one is compared with him.

plain_english: This advice works for our children. But for us adults, our upbringing and education are already done. We can't change our mistakes or take advice the same way. We have to work with what we've got now. We need to fight the root causes of anger. Anger starts when we believe someone has hurt us. So we shouldn't jump to that conclusion too quickly. We shouldn't get furious even when the injury seems obvious and clear. Some lies look like truth. We should always wait a bit. Time reveals what really happened. Don't listen too easily to gossip and accusations. We need to know this flaw in human nature: we want to believe things we don't want to hear. We get angry before we even know what we think. What can I say? We're swayed not just by slander but by suspicions. We might rage at innocent people just because of how they looked at us or smiled. We put the worst spin on everything. So we should defend the person who isn't here to defend themselves. Keep our anger on hold. You can always punish someone later, but once you've done it, you can't take it back.
original_excerpt: These precepts, however, apply to our children: in ourselves the accident of birth and our education no longer admits of either mistakes or advice; we must deal with what follows. Now we ought to fight against the first causes of evil: the cause of anger is the belief that we are injured; this belief, therefore, should not be lightly entertained. We ought not to fly into a rage even when the injury appears to be open and distinct: for some false things bear the semblance of truth. We should always allow some time to elapse, for time discloses the truth. Let not our ears be easily lent to calumnious talk: let us know and be on our guard against this fault of human nature, that we are willing to believe what we are unwilling to listen to, and that we become angry before we have formed our opinion. What shall I say? we are influenced not merely by calumnies but by suspicions, and at the very look and smile of others we may fly into a rage with innocent persons because we put the worst construction upon it. We ought, therefore, to plead the cause of the absent against ourselves, and to keep our anger in abeyance: for a punishment which has been postponed may yet be inflicted, but when once inflicted cannot be recalled.

plain_english:
Everyone knows the story of the would-be assassin who was caught before he could kill the tyrant. Under torture, Hippias tried to make him reveal his partners in the plot. But the assassin was clever. He named the tyrant's own friends — the very people standing around who cared most about keeping the tyrant alive. As the tyrant ordered each friend killed, the assassin was asked if anyone else remained. "Just you," he said. "I've killed everyone else who cared about you." The tyrant's anger had turned him into his own assassin's helper. He had cut down his own guards with his own sword.

How much braver was Alexander! His mother wrote warning him that his doctor Philip might poison him. But when Philip offered him medicine, Alexander drank it without fear.
